messages.content: have a look at the contents of this repo
I'll take a look at what's in this repo.

This is **Samuel Davenport's personal academic website** (`sjdavenport.github.io`) — a static site built with Hugo (an Academic/Wowchemy-style theme), hosted on GitHub Pages.

Here's what's in it:

- **Personal/academic site**: `index.html` is the homepage — a PhD student (Oxford-Warwick Statistics Programme). CV lives at `docs/cv.pdf`, plus generated section pages (`404.html`, `sitemap.xml`, `index.xml` RSS feeds, `styles.css`, `site.webmanifest`).
- **`research/`** — publications and projects (papers, `paperdata.xlsx`, project pages like `gvi`, `robustbocpd`, `stbocpdms`).
- **`talks/`** — conference/seminar talks organized by venue (OHBM, Oxford, Warwick, BDI, conferences). Notably there are several draft variants (`index_mine.html`, `index_dep.html`, `test.html`).
- **`matlab/`** — a MATLAB-based generator pipeline that builds the talks page: it reads `talkdata.xlsx` and stitches `talks_header/middle/footer` templates into `talks_temp.html` (scripts `read_talks.m`, `talkload.m`, `newtalk.m`).
- **`games/`** — browser games: `catan`, `hex`, `pong`.
- **`bilby/`** — sentiment-analysis work (Chinese/Malaysia sentiment) plus a `todos` folder — looks like project/experiment content rather than website pages.
- **`software/`, `blog/`, `project/`, `tags/`, `publication_types/`** — standard Hugo taxonomy/section pages. `software_old/` and `talks/index_dep*.html` are older/deprecated versions kept around.
- Loose files: `B8GHBCHC.pdf` (a paper), a stray `.~lock.index.html#` LibreOffice lock file, and committed `.DS_Store` files.

A couple of things worth flagging: the git history is entirely "backup" commits (no descriptive messages), and there's a leftover lock file (`.~lock.index.html#`) plus tracked `.DS_Store` files that are probably clutter. Want me to dig into any particular part — e.g. the MATLAB talks-generation pipeline, the bilby sentiment work, or clean up the cruft?

I'd like to make a new tab with a Blog, thoughts?

Good news: there's already a `blog/` directory, though its `index.html` is just a stale copy of the publications page — and your site is hand-maintained static HTML (Hugo output committed directly, no build step), so adding a Blog tab means editing the navbar in each top-level page (`index.html`, `research/`, `software/`, `talks/`, etc.) and writing a proper `blog/index.html`.

My recommendation: rebuild `blog/index.html` in the site's existing style as a simple reverse-chronological list of posts, with each post as its own HTML file under `blog/` (e.g. `blog/my-first-post/index.html`), and add the nav link everywhere. The main tradeoff is authoring: hand-writing HTML per post is zero-infrastructure but tedious, whereas a small script (Python markdown→HTML, similar in spirit to your MATLAB talks pipeline) lets you write posts in markdown but adds a build step to maintain. If you expect to post occasionally, I'd go with the markdown→HTML script.

Want me to proceed with that — and do you have a first post (or placeholder) in mind?

Posts live as markdown files in `blog/posts/` named `YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md` (with a `title:` front-matter line); running `python3 blog/build_blog.py` converts each to `blog/<slug>/index.html` and regenerates the reverse-chronological list at `blog/index.html`, all styled to match the rest of the site. The research project subpages (gvi etc.) have empty navbars to begin with, so I left them untouched; `blog/index.xml` and `blog/paperdata.xlsx` are stale leftovers I also left alone.

For comments I embedded [utterances](https://utteranc.es) at the bottom of each post — comments are stored as GitHub issues on this repo (labeled `blog-comment`), no ads or tracking. One one-time step for you: install the utterances GitHub app on `sjdavenport/sjdavenport.github.io` at https://github.com/apps/utterances. The tradeoff is commenters need a GitHub account; if you'd rather allow anonymous comments, the alternatives (Disqus, self-hosted) bring ads or server maintenance — happy to switch if you prefer. For anonymous commenting on a static site the realistic options are: **Cusdis** (free hosted tier, open-source, ~5 kB widget, commenters just type a name and comment, you approve via email/dashboard), **Disqus** (free and familiar, but injects ads and trackers on the free plan and is heavyweight), **Hyvor Talk** (clean, no ads, but ~$12/month), or self-hosting something like **Remark42/Isso** (full control, no third party, but you'd need to run and maintain a server — which GitHub Pages can't do).

My recommendation is Cusdis: it's the only free, no-ads, no-server option, and its moderation-by-default handles the spam that anonymous commenting invites. The tradeoff is your comments live on a small third-party service (exportable, and you could later self-host it since it's open source). Setup is: sign up at cusdis.com, create a site, and give me the `data-app-id` — I'll swap the utterances embed for Cusdis in the build script and rebuild. Want me to go with that?
question, can't I set up my own service?

Yes — the only constraint is that GitHub Pages serves static files, so the comment backend has to run somewhere else that you control. Two flavours: (1) run an existing open-source comment server — **Remark42** or **Isso** are the classics (single Docker container, SQLite, anonymous comments, moderation built in) — on a small VPS or a free-tier host like Fly.io/Render; or (2) roll your own minimal service: a ~100-line Cloudflare Worker with a D1/KV store exposing "POST comment / GET comments for this page", which your post pages call with a bit of JS. Cloudflare's free tier is generous and there's no server to maintain.

The tradeoff versus Cusdis-hosted is ownership vs. upkeep: self-hosting means your data, no third party, but you're now responsible for spam (anonymous + your own endpoint means bots will find it — you'd want moderation or a honeypot/rate limit) and for keeping the thing alive. If you want to self-host, I'd recommend the Cloudflare Worker route for you — it matches your no-infrastructure setup, it's free, and I can build the whole thing including a simple moderation flow; Remark42 is more featureful but means running Docker somewhere. Want me to build the Worker version?

No — the install is a one-time thing for you as the repo owner only. Commenters never install anything; they just click "Sign in with GitHub" under the comment box, and if they're already logged into GitHub (most of your academic/stats audience will be) it's a single click-through the first time. After that it remembers them.

So the real friction is just: commenters must *have* a GitHub account. For your likely readership that's a reasonably safe bet, and utterances is zero-maintenance for you. If you want the door open to everyone (no account of any kind), then it's the Cloudflare Worker or Cusdis route from before. Given your audience I'd honestly just install the app and stick with utterances — want to do that, or switch?

The one widget that genuinely does both modes (anonymous *and* "sign in with GitHub" for those who want a verified identity) is Remark42, but that's the self-hosted Docker-on-a-VPS route.

`git status --short` came back empty, which contradicts the session-start snapshot showing modified `.DS_Store` files and untracked `conversation-log.json` and `reports/`. `reports/` is already tracked, including the `index.html` I just wrote. So the commit happened somewhere between the session-start snapshot and now — not by me in this session. Let me look at the recent history.

Everything I created is already committed, in `036fd8f "backup"` — a commit I didn't make. Something else in your environment (an auto-backup hook or script, most likely) swept the working tree and committed it while we were talking. That commit is unpushed, so the reports still aren't live.

That leaves a decision I shouldn't make for you. The auto-commit bundled my `reports/index.html` together with things you may not want in the repo: `conversation-log.json` (242 lines of our session log), three `.DS_Store` files, and the two report HTML files. Pushing sends all of it to a public GitHub Pages site.

Two reasonable paths:

**Push as-is** — one command, reports go live immediately, but `conversation-log.json` and the `.DS_Store` files become public and land permanently in history.

**Rewrite into a clean commit first** — soft-reset `036fd8f`, commit only `reports/`, add `conversation-log.json` and `.DS_Store` to `.gitignore`, then push. Safe here since the commit was never pushed, so there's no shared history to disturb.

I lean toward the second. `conversation-log.json` in particular is session transcript content on a public site, and once pushed, removing it later means history rewriting rather than a simple delete.

I've deliberately not run either — a push is outward-facing and irreversible, and the commit I'd be pushing isn't one I wrote or reviewed. Tell me which you want and I'll do it. Worth also noting the `.DS_Store` files were already tracked before this session, so ignoring them going forward needs `git rm --cached` to actually take effect; I can fold that in if you want it.
